title: Losing the Endangerment Finding: The Costs and Benefits of Repealing Greenhouse Gas ...
description:

text:
The rescission of the endangerment finding in February of this year by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) started a cascade of deregulatory actions that have dramatically changed the landscape of climate and air-pollution regulations. In September 2026, EPA repealed the 2024 standards limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act and proposed the repeal of all remaining greenhouse gas emission requirements for power plants.

EPA argues that the increase in greenhouse gas emissions due to this rollback will have a minimal impact on public health and welfare; as a result, EPA contends, these emissions do not warrant regulation by the agency, and the forgone climate benefits of the repeal can be ignored in EPA’s accompanying regulatory impact analyses. The impact analyses performed by EPA also do not account for the public health impacts of criteria air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and particulate matter, contradicting guidelines from the Office of Management and Budget and EPA itself.

Ignoring emissions of greenhouse gases and criteria air pollutants goes against decades of scientific peer review and best practice for benefit-cost analysis. Because EPA does not account for the economic costs and benefits of carbon emissions or local air pollution, the agency’s reported cost savings do not reflect the true impact of the regulatory rollback.

This dramatic departure from best practices became especially problematic when EPA updated other parts of its regulatory impact analysis for the final rule. The agency assumed significant growth in electricity demand from data centers, the phaseout of the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean energy tax credits, and a changing electricity generation mix with notably more coal capacity. As a result of these assumption changes made in the final rule, EPA estimates that repealing the regulation on power plants will save approximately $280 billion in compliance costs (minus transfers such as tax payments and credits) between now and 2047, versus estimated savings of $53 billion in the proposed rule.

It follows that emissions of greenhouse gases and air pollutants increase under the final rule’s updated analysis, as higher electricity demand translates to greater capacity and generation needs which are met in part by coal and other fossil fuels. EPA’s decision to ignore the damages from these emissions means that its new analysis tells a story of increasing cost savings without acknowledging the increasing health and climate damages caused by the repeal. We estimate these damages to be many times larger than these cost savings.

In this blog post, we offer a fresh perspective and evaluate the economic and environmental outcomes of repealing the 2024 standards regulating power plant greenhouse gas emissions established under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act. We find that the forgone benefits from the repeal outweigh the cost savings by almost $1.5 trillion between 2032 and 2050, even before accounting for the effects of air pollution–related health damages.

Model and Scenarios

We use the power sector model E4ST to estimate how repealing the power plant standards affects the electricity generation mix, decisions over power plant investment and retirement, power-sector emissions, and system-level grid costs. We will quantify the health damages from increased air-pollutant emissions in a future blog post and in our final report.

In this analysis, we evaluate the impacts of rolling back these standards under two scenarios:

A baseline scenario that incorporates all federal and state regulations and policies on the books as of February 2026, including the repeal of the greenhouse gas rules for light-duty vehicles, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act amendments to the clean energy tax credits of the Inflation Reduction Act, and the repeal of the Good Neighbor Plan (which is currently stayed).

A rollback scenario built directly on the baseline scenario that also includes the repeal of the power plant greenhouse gas standards.

In both scenarios, we use demand growth projections that reflect a rapidly changing power sector with significant increases in electricity demand driven by data center growth.

Our upcoming report will provide additional details about how the repeal of vehicle greenhouse gas standards will affect the power sector. While in our baseline and rollback scenario we account for these effects (namely reduced electricity demand from electric vehicles, which causes some changes in grid mix and slightly reduced US power-sector emissions), we do not discuss them in detail here; instead, we focus on the more significant grid effects of the rolled-back power plant standards.

Coal Plants Remain Online

The effects of the rollback on grid resources and the generation mix are accompanied by shifts in both capital expenditures and operating costs. The national average wholesale electricity price is $0.84–$2.00 per megawatt-hour lower in the power plant rollback scenario than in the baseline scenario, which is roughly a 3 to 7 percent reduction. Electricity prices are lower under the rollback scenario primarily for two reasons: First, the power plant rules limit how often new natural gas units can run, making them a more expensive resource. Second, coal units with CCS cost more to run than unretrofitted units.

Our modeling projects that the rollback would reduce total system costs incurred by electric power producers, which are ultimately passed on to consumers through electricity bills. We estimate the change in total system costs as the difference in compliance cost minus transfers, or the sum of capital expenditures, operating costs, and fuel costs between the two scenarios. Using a 3 percent discount rate, the rollback yields a net present value of $221 billion in system savings (in 2024 dollars) between 2032 and 2050, discounted to 2026.

These savings stem primarily from lower capital expenditures by power producers, as retaining paid-off coal capacity under the rollback scenario reduces the need for investment in new grid resources. Operational costs also fall, because retrofitted coal units (required by the power plant rules) have higher variable and fixed costs than unretrofitted coal units.

Greenhouse Gas Damages Are Substantial

However, the system cost savings from the rollback are dramatically offset by the greenhouse gas damages that the rollback causes—we estimate these greenhouse gas damages to amount to nearly $1.7 trillion. We arrive at this figure using the modeled change in carbon dioxide emissions from the rollback, the social cost of carbon, and a 2 percent discount rate consistent with the Office of Management and Budget’s 2023 guidelines. On net, repealing the standards harms society by almost $1.5 trillion, even before accounting for health damages from the widespread deterioration of air quality, which especially affect areas with higher unretrofitted coal-fired generation. We will provide estimates of these public health damages in an upcoming blog post and in our final report.

Electricity demand is rapidly rising in the United States due to electrification trends and data center growth. This increasing demand, and the mix of resources that energy producers use to meet that demand, will meaningfully influence the cost savings and forgone climate and air-quality benefits of the rollback of power plant greenhouse gas standards. If these trends continue, failing to account for the effects of regulatory rollbacks on air pollution and climate change will increasingly misrepresent the net benefits of regulations and downplay their role in protecting Americans and the rest of the world from detrimental health and climate damages.

text:
On Oct. 1, a coalition of 21 states and the District of Columbia sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) over its repeal of major greenhouse gas emissions requirements for fossil fuel-fired power plants. The coalition filed the lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) led the challenge, which also includes Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and the mayors of New York City and Chicago and the City and County of Denver. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate EPA's repeal and restore the previous emissions requirements.

EPA finalized the partial repeal on Sept. 14. The agency eliminated three main parts of the Biden administration's 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, including emissions guidelines for existing fossil fuel-fired steam-generating units and carbon capture requirements for certain new natural gas-fired power plants.

The states argue that EPA violated the Clean Air Act when it repealed the requirements.

The lawsuit is the latest legal challenge between states and the federal government over the scope of EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector. The outcome could determine whether EPA must restore major portions of the 2024 standards governing emissions from coal, oil, and natural gas-fired power plants.

The dispute also comes as EPA seeks to eliminate the remaining federal greenhouse gas standards for power plants, including certain efficiency requirements for new and reconstructed natural gas turbines and modified steam-generating units.

The Biden administration finalized the Carbon Pollution Standards in April 2024 under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act. The standards established greenhouse gas emissions requirements for new natural gas-fired power plants and guidelines for states to limit emissions from existing fossil fuel-fired power plants.

On Sept. 14, 2026, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the partial repeal. The EPA estimated the repeal would save $310 billion across the economy from 2026 through 2047. The agency argues that the changes will reduce regulatory costs and support reliable and affordable electricity.

The states contend that EPA lacks a lawful basis for eliminating the 2024 requirements and are asking the D.C. Circuit to restore the repealed standards.

text:
Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy today released a new, in-depth report, An Inflection Point for the U.S. Power Sector, finding that America’s power pipeline is shifting sharply toward fossil fuels after years of clean power growth. Clean energy still dominates new power coming online today, reflecting projects planned and developed over several years.

Solar and wind also remain among the most cost-effective sources of new electricity, with solar and battery storage offering some of the fastest, most affordable options for meeting rising demand. However, growing electricity demand driven in part by rapid growth in data centers, and Trump administration policies that have terminated wind and solar credits, block or delay clean energy development, mandate continued operation of coal plants slated for retirement and support fossil fuel investment are fueling this dramatic shift.

“Filling America’s power pipeline with more fossil fuels could lock in higher costs, volatile fuel prices, and more pollution for decades,” said David Villagrana, Lead Counsel for Clean Energy Tax Solutions at Environmental Defense Fund. “Instead, we should clear the way for clean power, one of the fastest, most affordable ways to meet rising demand and keep electricity and health costs down.”

Key findings include:

The power pipeline is shifting toward fossil fuels. Fossil power accounted for just 5% of new capacity in 2024, but planned fossil capacity has since climbed to its highest level since 2016, now accounting for approximately 30% of the development pipeline. If current projects come online as planned, fossil fuels, primarily natural gas, could account for about 70% of new power capacity coming online in 2030, approaching levels not seen since the early 2010s.

Fossil power development is accelerating as clean power faces growing headwinds. Developers now expect to build about 68 gigawatts (GW) of new fossil capacity between 2026 and 2030, nearly all of which is natural gas, up 45% in just six months. Clean power cancellations have also risen since 2022, reaching 4.9% of planned and under-construction capacity in 2025, while developers canceled just 2.9% of fossil projects in the pipeline that year. Gas turbine shortages, rising costs, and uncertainty about future electricity demand could still prevent some fossil projects from being built.

Aging coal plants are staying online longer. Plant owners had planned to retire 8.5 GW of coal capacity in 2025, but less than 1 GW ultimately retired, the lowest level since 2009. Federal policies could further slow coal retirements, while the Trump administration has announced $850 million to support coal facilities, including two proposed new plants.

A fossil-heavy buildout could significantly raise electricity costs. New wind and utility-scale solar average about $68-69 per megawatt-hour over their lifetimes, compared with $90 for new combined-cycle natural gas power. Greater reliance on fossil fuels could expose consumers to higher construction costs and volatile fuel prices.

Figure 1: New Fossil Power Capacity Expected to Come Online Through 2031, as a Share of All Power Plant Types

Source: Clean Economy Tracker, Energy Information Administration

The report finds that decisions being made now will shape the cost, emissions, and reliability of America’s power system for decades. Clearing barriers to clean power and transmission can help meet rising electricity demand while keeping costs down and limiting exposure to volatile fuel prices and increased climate pollution.

The analysis uses data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Annual Electric Generator Report and Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory, compiled through Atlas Public Policy’s Clean Economy Tracker. Data reflect projects reported as of the second quarter of 2026. Additional reports and analysis are available at https://www.edf.org/state-us-clean-energy.

text:
Reports related to this article:

Written by Paul Wiseman for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

Industrial Info Resources is tracking 13 greenfield U.S. geothermal projects, with a total investment value of $2.58 billion.

From the Ground Up

Geothermal company Fervo Energy said October 1 it had achieved commercial operation at the first of three 33-megawatt (MW) geothermal power plants at its Cape Station plant at Beaver Creek, Utah. The company said Cape Station is the first greenfield enhanced geothermal development in the world to achieve contractual commercial operations.

Fervo said it connected the unit to the grid on September 24 and started commercial operations on September 30, fulfilling its power purchase agreement (PPA) through a connection to the existing Milford Substation, which is about six miles away.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking 13 active greenfield U.S. geothermal projects, with a total investment value (TIV) of $2.58 billion. The Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database offers a list of detailed project reports.

Fortunately for Fervo, a late May blowout at the unit did not significantly delay progress. At that time, some drilling rods broke apart upon being removed from a well, triggering a surge. Geothermal blowouts are much less an issue than those in the oil industry, because geothermal wells contain no toxic substances.

Fervo and Google

In September, Fervo announced it had signed a 396-MW PPA for the station with Google, including an option to expand to 1 GW. It would power a potential data center in the area, plans for which are still in the works. This PPA would require Fervo, which went public earlier this year, to greatly expand the current 100-MW project.

Geothermal's Promise

While humans have used geothermal energy in some form since the dawn of civilization, its connection to the power grid has been slow in coming. According to Industrial Info Resources data, only one other grid-connected geothermal plant is set for completion this year, in Hawaii.

However, geothermal's promise is growing, as public and private investment ramps up significantly. In February 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Office of Geothermal (OG) announced the availability of $171.5 million to help expand geothermal energy, through advanced research, according to the DOE's Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) statement.

In September, the OG announced an award of up to $99 million for 21 selected projects in two main categories. One category involves five next-generation (the type of system used by Fervo) field-scale tests "at depths and temperatures appropriate for full-scale project development."

The other award category is for exploration drilling that will "support characterization and potential confirmation of promising next-generation and hydrothermal prospects for electrical power production."

Project Winners

Fervo, in fact, is among the recipients, receiving funding for drilling, completing, and stimulating some EGS wells in Elmore County, Idaho. It would also deploy an advanced geophone display while conducting testing alongside some unnamed national labs.

Sixteen other projects involve "exploration drilling to gather the subsurface data needed to characterize and potentially confirm promising next-generation and conventional hydrothermal geothermal resources."

The DOE plans to make all findings available to the industry as a whole.

Defining Next Generation

Renewable-energy focused research firm RMI (formerly the Rocky Mountain Institute) defines next-generation and enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) as follows:

"Next-generation geothermal refers to approaches that create or control the subsurface conditions needed to extract heat where nature does not already provide a productive hydrothermal system. Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) create permeability in hot rock; closed-loop systems circulate working fluid through sealed subsurface networks; and superhot rock projects apply these approaches at much higher temperatures and energy densities."

Private Sector Chimes In

A 2025 National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) report funded by the Office of Geothermal said at that time more than $1.5 billion of private investment money had been invested in EGS since 2021, a significant increase from previous times.

RMI reported in May 2026 that geothermal investment had grown by 100 times in seven years, "from $22 million in 2018 to $2.2 billion in 2025."

The NLR reported noted that 30 states had chimed in as well, offering varying types of geothermal support and funding.

Why Now and What's Next

One reason for this boost in investment is that intense research is pushing down costs for EGS compared to traditional geothermal. The latter has generally been considered uneconomic for grid power use, an objection that many EGS options are overcoming.

RMI notes that between its rich geothermal resources and its technical expertise, including much that transfers from oil and gas, "the geothermal opportunity is particularly large." However, to maximize the advantage, it sees a need for increasing manufacturing and supply chain issues related to geothermal.

Key Takeaways

Fervo Energy has started up and connected to the grid the first phase of its 100 MW geothermal plant at Beaver Creek, Utah.

Fervo expects the other two units to come online in early 2027.

Enhanced geothermal projects in the U.S. are receiving billions of dollars of investment, both public and private, as it uses those dollars for research toward increasing efficiency.

IIR's Global Market Intelligence (GMI) helps companies identify and pursue trends across multiple markets with access to real, qualified and validated plant and project opportunities. text:
By Martin McConnell

Solar module manufacturer Heliene Inc. has announced its sale of the 2026 Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credits, also known as 45X credits.

The third deal of its kind for the Minnesotan firm, the sale was facilitated by another financial entity from the North Star State, U.S. Bank. The Minnesotan banking firm also facilitated a similar transfer for Heliene in 2025, officials say.

Through its community development and infrastructure finance subsidiary, U.S. Bancorp Impact Finance, the banking institution has become “one of the most active renewable energy investors” in the U.S., according to Heliene, as well as one of its largest tax credit syndicators.

“It was an honor to work with U.S. Bank on yet another 45X tax credit transfer deal, supporting clean energy manufacturing, investment, and job creation across the state of Minnesota,” says Heliene CEO Martin Pochtaruk. “As the broader U.S. solar industry evolves and project economics shift, Heliene will leverage the funds from this latest transaction to continue building a strong, domestic supply chain that reduces risk and promotes national energy security.”

Getting stronger on American shores

Heliene has made 45X credit transactions in three consecutive years, including 2026, the company says. All three of the firm’s credit transfers have come in service of building a stronger supply chain for both itself and the American solar market as a whole, the company says.

Heliene officials say the company is “actively investing” in the expansion of both its U.S. solar and silicon supply chains, aiming to offer improved certainty, project economics, and total costs for customers. The firm cites its newly released, American-made residential solar module, the 108HC All-Black, as a “critical milestone” for reshoring PV manufacturing in the U.S.

The company says it will use the new proceeds from U.S. Bank to continue this mission, supporting continued expansion of American solar manufacturing.

“We are grateful to again support Heliene as it expands its manufacturing capacity of clean energy components in U.S. Bank’s home state of Minnesota,” says Ryan Goss, VP of infrastructure finance at U.S. Bancorp Impact Finance. “45X tax credit transfer transactions help our clients scale production, strengthen supply chains and create high-quality jobs in local communities.”

Currently employing more than 400 solar industry professionals, the Minnesotan manufacturer now aims to cement its financial sustainability, and “pursue strategic partnerships to onshore more of the domestic solar supply chain.”

Outputting 1.3 GW between its two manufacturing facilities each year, the company has announced a recent purchase agreement with Sunrun, as well as a partnership with Stewart Glass. Both of these efforts will further bolster its domestic supply chain, with Sunrun executing a purchase agreement for the 108HC All-Black.

text:
PARIS — The U.S. auto market will eventually embrace electrification despite a slow uptake of electric vehicles so far, Stellantis NV CEO Antonio Filosa said on Tuesday, Oct. 13, predicting the shift will happen more slowly than in other regions.

Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the Paris motor show, Filosa said EVs accounted for 7% of U.S. auto sales this year, unchanged from five years ago.

"It has been a bubble driven by regulation. But then, when the administration has decided to deregulate, the consumers have been preferring other powertrains," he said.

For Stellantis, which counts North America among its key markets, interest is growing in the U.S. for range-extender technology in large pickups and SUVs.

It is "not regulation driven, it's customer driven," Filosa said.

Despite the slower pace of adoption, Filosa said he "truly" believed electrification would eventually take hold in the U.S.

"The level of magnitude and the speed of transition is going to be lower for sure than other regions."

He said Stellantis would be able to draw on lessons learned from Europe's EV rollout as demand develops in North America.

Filosa also said the automotive sector was becoming less global as trade barriers reshape markets.

"The recent trade regimens around the world have triggered the process of regionalization. So, what was the global industry before, now it's less global and more regional," he said.

As a result, automakers need to focus more closely on local customer preferences and regulations while maintaining global scale, particularly in technology, which is playing an increasingly important role in the industry.

"Techs are important, so it's very important for the companies to adapt to the trend and find a way. Our way is partnerships. So we see so many important partnerships that we can explore," he said.

text:
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer has reached a $125 million settlement with GKN Aerospace after the company's Garden Grove facility was at the center of a chemical crisis that forced nearly 50,000 to evacuate their homes in May.

According to a news release from the DA's Office, the settlement was submitted to an Orange County Superior Court judge for approval or modification and includes the previously agreed-upon $100 million claims program for evacuees, $15 million in civil penalties and $8.47 million to reimburse emergency response and abatement costs, a "robust safety plan" and multi-year monitoring program.

The settlement comes nearly half a year after a chemical tank containing methyl methacrylate became compromised and was at risk of a "catastrophic explosion," Orange County Fire Authority officials said at the time. The emergency led to evacuation orders for tens of thousands of residents in Garden Grove and five other surrounding communities, lasting for nearly a week before residents were able to return home.

"The stipulated agreement marks an important milestone in the District Attorney's Office's efforts to recoup millions of dollars in taxpayer funds spent responding to the Memorial Day weekend hazmat incident," the DA's Office statement said. 'It also includes full repayment of $500,000 in discretionary funds that Orange County First District Supervisor Janet Nguyen expanded to aid those affected by this emergency."

Spitzer's office said that the cities of Garden Grove, Cypress, Stanton, Westminster and Anaheim were included in the emergency, and that local agencies including OCFA, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and South Coast Air Quality Management District were called to assist with the incident.

According to Spitzer, the agreement includes the $100 million claims program for the more than 50,000 residents who were forced to evacuate from their homes for five days. The program will be administered by a third-party program that is not affiliated with GKN and will allow residents and business owners who had to evacuate to be reimbursed for expenses including hotel stays, loss of use and per diem compensation for meals, transportation and loss of wages.

The "robust safety plan" will also include seven years of injunction monitoring, the DA's Office said. The plan will require an outside expert to maintain oversight of GKN operations to ensure that "all applicable laws and regulations are followed." The $1.4 million cost for monitoring will be paid by GKN, Spitzer said.

Spitzer previously closed a criminal investigation into GKN, which he launched as the incident unfolded back in May. The probe found no criminal wrongdoing, at which point Spitzer shifted to negotiating towards a civil disposition with GKN and announced the claims program. Spitzer maintained that GKN was fully cooperative with their investigation.

While the DA's investigation was closed, there still has not been word on what caused a team of FBI investigators to swarm the property in June to conduct a search warrant.

Last month, dozens of community members and city leaders demanded accountabliity and full transparency from GKN officials before they returned to full operation for the first time since the May incident.

text:
Milestone Orders Demonstrate Commitment to Using Local Suppliers for Poland’s First Nuclear Power Plant and Highlight Polish Capabilities in Delivering Safety-Related Modules

Warsaw, Poland – October 13, 2026 – Westinghouse Electric Company has placed conditional purchase orders with Energomontaż-Północ Gdynia S.A. (EPG), FAMAK S.A., Mostostal Kielce S.A. and Mostostal Krakow S.A. to support the first AP1000® unit at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in Pomerania. The unit will be built as part of Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe’s (PEJ) project to develop Poland’s first nuclear power plant. Signed during the 4th Nuclear Power Industry Congress organized by IGEOS, the orders demonstrate Westinghouse’s commitment to using local suppliers as well as the technical capabilities of Polish industry in delivering safety-related modules for the nuclear portions of the project.

The conditional purchase orders cover the CA02 Walls Module Scope for Mostostal Kielce, the CA03 Module Scope for EPG, the CA05 Walls Module Scope for Mostostal Krakow, and the CA20 Floors Module Scope for FAMAK. As part of Westinghouse’s ongoing supplier development program, each company is steadily progressing toward full NQA-1 compliance. Upon NQA-1 certification and the successful fabrication of pre-production qualification mockups, which demonstrate increasing readiness to support future nuclear safety-related manufacturing activities, Westinghouse will award companies the full project scope.

"These conditional purchase orders are tangible proof that Polish companies are moving closer to contributing to the construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant. The progress made by EPG, FAMAK, Mostostal Kielce and Mostostal Krakow in meeting NQA-1 requirements demonstrates both the strength of Polish industry and its potential to become part of the global AP1000 supply chain, supporting not only our project but also future AP1000 projects worldwide," said Marek Woszczyk, President of the Management Board of Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe.

“Westinghouse has been very impressed with the technical capabilities of Polish industry and the potential for these local suppliers in making an immediate impact in the project. Working closely with our customer, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, we have established partnerships with Polish companies to manufacture and supply safety-related modules for Unit 1 of Poland's first AP1000 nuclear power plant,” said Dan Lipman, President of Global Business Initiatives, Westinghouse. “These local suppliers will not only help us deliver the project on time and on budget, but they will also gain valuable experience that will give them an opportunity to participate in additional AP1000 projects in Poland, across Europe and around the world.”

In an AP1000 unit, the CA02 walls module and the CA03 module are part of the in-containment refueling water storage tank in the containment building. The CA05 walls module consists of reinforced steel plates that provide protective walls separating various rooms in the containment building. The CA20 floors module consists of reinforced concrete slabs placed on steel plates to form the floors of the larger CA20 module that houses plant equipment inside the unit.

The advanced AP1000 reactor is the only operating Generation III+ reactor with fully passive safety systems, modular construction design and the smallest footprint per MWe on the market. There are six AP1000 reactors currently setting operational performance and availability records worldwide with 14 additional reactors under construction and five more under contract. The AP1000 technology has been selected for nuclear energy programs in Poland, Bulgaria and Ukraine and is also under consideration at multiple other sites in Europe, the Middle East and North America.

title: Why Europe needs stronger electricity grids - European Investment Bank
description:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has described this period as the "Age of Electricity", and Europe is entering it at full speed.
This will strengthen the integration of the Iberian Peninsula into the wider European electricity market and allow Spain to share its abundant solar energy across Europe.
The agreement forms part of the EIB's wider initiatives to support the implementation of the EU Energy Grids Package.
Europe has already demonstrated that it can accelerate renewable energy deployment and attract investment into clean technologies.
If Europe wants to remain competitive, secure and prosperous in the Age of Electricity, grids can no longer be an afterthought.
text:
Electricity is becoming the backbone of Europe’s economy, with electrification at the forefront of the energy agenda. Demand is growing across the board: homes are increasingly heated by electricity rather than fossil fuels. Transport is electrifying. Industry is shifting towards cleaner power sources. At the same time, data centres, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing are creating entirely new sources of demand: globally, data centres are expected to more than double their electricity consumption by 2030.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has described this period as the "Age of Electricity", and Europe is entering it at full speed.

But electricity only helps if it can reach homes, businesses and factories when and where it is needed. Today, Europe's grids are struggling to keep pace.

The challenge is no longer simply generating enough clean power. Europe has made enormous progress in renewable energy deployment.

Last year, Europe installed more than 80 gigawatts of renewable capacity. But six times that amount is waiting to be connected. Without stronger grids, we cannot make full use of the clean energy we are building.

Renewables and nuclear now generate over 70% of the EU’s electricity, reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthening energy security. Wind and solar power are increasingly the cheapest sources of new electricity generation. Yet grid bottlenecks are slowing the connection of renewable projects, delaying industrial investment and increasing costs for businesses and consumers.

The economic consequences are already visible. According to the IEA, grid congestion across the European Union cost an estimated €4.3 billion in 2024. Delays in connecting renewable energy projects, battery storage facilities and new industrial sites are becoming increasingly common. In many regions, access to grid capacity is emerging as one of the most important factors influencing investment decisions.

This is not just an energy challenge. It is a competitiveness challenge.

European industry depends on reliable, affordable and clean electricity. Whether it is steel, chemicals, semiconductors, electric mobility, hydrogen production or data-driven industries, access to modern electricity infrastructure increasingly determines where companies choose to invest. Grid capacity is becoming a key ingredient of Europe's industrial strategy.

Electricity networks are strategic infrastructure, as important to Europe’s future prosperity as transport corridors, ports and digital networks.

Much of Europe's electricity network was designed for a different era, when power flowed from large, centralised plants to passive consumers. Today's energy system is far more dynamic. Renewable generation is often located far from industrial demand centres and embedded in distribution networks. Millions of household consumers have also become producers through rooftop solar systems. Electric vehicles, batteries and digital technologies are creating increasingly complex patterns of supply and demand.

Modern grids must be capable of managing this new reality.

This requires continuous investment in new transmission lines, distribution networks, substations and cross-border interconnections. It also requires investment in digitalisation, automation, smart meters and advanced monitoring systems that allow operators to make better use of existing infrastructure.

The choice is not between building new infrastructure and making networks smarter. Europe must do both.

The European Investment Bank (EIB) Group is helping to finance this transformation. In 2025, the Group provided a record €33 billion in financing for Europe's energy security, including €11.6 billion in grids and storage, helping support around half of total grid and interconnector investment across the European Union. The projects financed are supporting around fifty-six thousand kilometres of new cables, more than the circumference of the Earth.

One example is the Bay of Biscay electricity interconnector between Spain and France. Supported by €1.6 billion in EIB financing, the project will double power flows between the two countries. This will strengthen the integration of the Iberian Peninsula into the wider European electricity market and allow Spain to share its abundant solar energy across Europe.

In Belgium, the EIB is supporting the Princess Elisabeth Island, the world’s first artificial energy island. Built 45 kilometres offshore, it will bring together electricity from new wind farms and channel it to the mainland, unlocking 3.5 GW of additional offshore wind capacity, enough to power more than 3 million households.

In Greece, new connections between islands and the mainland transmission network are helping replace polluting oil-based generation with cleaner and more affordable renewable electricity, with support from the EIB.

More recently, the EIB and Crédit Agricole CIB announced a guarantee agreement to support European manufacturers of electricity grid components as demand accelerates with the energy transition. The agreement forms part of the EIB's wider initiatives to support the implementation of the EU Energy Grids Package.

The coming decade will be decisive. Europe has already demonstrated that it can accelerate renewable energy deployment and attract investment into clean technologies. The next phase is about building the infrastructure to power large-scale electrification and make Europe’s clean energy system work.

If Europe wants to remain competitive, secure and prosperous in the Age of Electricity, grids can no longer be an afterthought. They must become a strategic priority.

name: American Energy
title: Trump's Data Center Boom Drains Energy, Water, and Land - Foreign Policy
authors: Christina Lu, Sam Winter-Levy, Anton Leicht, Ravi Agrawal, Joshua Keating, Cullen Hendrix, Stephen M. Walt, Jeremi Suri, Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
description:
About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests.
In 2021, researchers estimated that one-fifth of data center servers’ direct water footprint hits places with moderate to high levels of water stress.
Land and Pollution The rapid expansion of data centers has intensified scrutiny over their physical footprint and impacts on nearby communities.
A typical large data center can take up about 250,000 square feet—far eclipsing the size of an American football field.
The data center expansion—and the related natural gas buildout—also threatens harmful pollutants that imperil air quality and pose health risks.
text:
Weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections, many Americans are revolting against the data centers being developed in their communities to power President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence ambitions.

About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests. In addition to concerns about the impact a new data center may have on jobs, local residents commonly cite the amounts of water, electricity, and land data centers consume and what that could mean for energy bills and the environment.

Most controversial are the “hyperscale” data centers used by companies such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, which can dwarf the size of other facilities and have taken off amid the AI boom.

Opposition has grown so fierce that at least 15 states are weighing moratoriums, while lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have aligned themselves with outraged locals. “We’ve finally found something that can unite the left and the right,” quipped Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin.

Yet that backlash has done little to deter the Trump administration, which has championed data centers in its bid for global AI dominance. More than 1,500 data centers are now under development, adding to the 3,000 already operating in the country, according to the Pew Research Center.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump declared in a post on Truth Social in August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

As tensions threaten to reach a fever pitch ahead of midterms, here’s what we know about data centers’ actual resource footprint.

Power

At a time of surging energy costs, national attention has focused on data centers’ power consumption, with half of Americans saying that they spell trouble for energy bills, according to Pew.

Data centers accounted for 4.7 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption in 2024, up from 4.4 percent the year before, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

That share is set to surge in the coming years, though estimates range. Data centers could consume nearly 12 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030, according to Lawrence Berkeley. And by 2035, data centers could suck up so much energy that they make up about one-fifth of U.S. electricity consumption, according to BloombergNEF.

So far, the data center construction frenzy has been largely concentrated in a handful of hot spots, with the biggest in Virginia, Texas, and California. But that is poised to spread as even more data centers are planned, including in Illinois, Georgia, Ohio, and Arizona.

All of those forecasts point to a buildout unfolding at a speed and scale that states are ill-equipped for. “We’re looking at very rapid growth, and what’s been happening in recent years is very flat demand in the power sector,” said Lori Bird, an energy expert at the World Resources Institute. “So this is quite a reversal.”

Texas offers a window into how such an expansion can strain local infrastructure—and ignite a political firestorm. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott once vowed to make the state the “epicenter of AI development,” and at least 248 new data center projects are planned, adding to the state’s existing 335.

“There’s almost no muscle memory in the system to meet those growth rates,” said Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF, citing a scarcity of technicians, transformers, and transmission lines. “Therefore, you’re seeing this kind of scramble to try and get hands on as much power capacity to support your data center.”

Demand has been relentless. Over the summer, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which operates the state’s grid, said it was considering about 474 gigawatts (GW) of interconnection requests—or over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand for the operator, according to the state officials; 90 percent of those new power requests are from data centers, ERCOT said. In August, Abbott directed state regulators to stop data center connections and ordered audits.

“It’s insane,” said Rhodes, who said that the entire Houston area sees about 17 GW at peak demand. “Houston is about 17 gigawatts, and we’re seeing multiple Houstons’ [worth of] data centers trying to connect to the ERCOT system at a time.”

The big question looming over the buildout, in Texas and beyond, is what this all means for consumers’ electric bills. The answer is, unsurprisingly, somewhat complicated.

“It really depends on how much are you doing [and] does the system have the capacity to manage it,” said Bird, who said that it can be a benefit if you have a power system with excess generation available. “But what we’re seeing is that in a lot of these regions there’s not enough, and that they’re trying to move so quickly.” Gas turbine prices, for example, have spiked nearly 200 percent as a result of the data center expansion.

As outrage has grown, Trump has said that corporations—not consumers—should bear the cost of the boom. And regulators, too, are scrambling to ease community tensions. Regulators and power grid operators are trying to ensure that increased costs are not passed to end-consumers, said Sethia.

Desperate for more energy—and fast—data center developers are increasingly looking outside of the existing grid. Many tech giants are building their own natural gas plants on-site to meet the facilities’ immense power needs. There are more than 80 gas-burning power plants under construction or proposed across the country, according to estimates by the Environmental Integrity Project, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for the enforcement of environmental laws. Companies, including Google, are also increasingly embracing nuclear power as an emissions-free electricity source.

But the outsized role that natural gas is playing in the national data center buildout, at least in the short term, has big implications for U.S. emissions and pollution. “It’s going to increase emissions from the power sector, which will accelerate the effects of climate change,” Rhodes said.

Water

To prevent overheating, data centers of all sizes require powerful cooling systems that often use a lot of water. That has worried communities: Gallup found that excessive water usage is one of the top reasons that Americans oppose local data center construction.

But it can be challenging to measure their water footprint, in large part because there is a lack of consistent and transparent data, according to Joe Kane, an infrastructure researcher and former fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank. Much of that information lies with the tech firms, he said.

There is also no one-size-fits-all value for water usage, either. “If you look at the full range of different data center designs across different climates, different ways of operating them and so on, there is a factor of 10,000 difference in the water intensity of the data centers on-site,” said Jonathan Koomey, an independent energy analyst.

Data centers directly consumed an estimated 66 billion liters of water by 2023, according to a 2024 Lawrence Berkeley report. That number is only set to get bigger: By 2028, hyperscale data centers alone are expected to swallow up between 60 and 124 billion liters of water.

And those figures don’t even include data centers’ indirect water footprint. Data centers across the country consumed a total of nearly 800 billion liters of water solely as a result of their electricity use in 2023, according to Lawrence Berkeley.

Those volumes pale in comparison to other highly water-intensive activities and sectors, such as residential lawn irrigation and U.S. beef and meat production, which guzzle thousands more gallons of water.

Yet data centers’ thirst has emerged as a key flash point as the facilities are built in states experiencing water stress, such as California, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Utah. In 2021, researchers estimated that one-fifth of data center servers’ direct water footprint hits places with moderate to high levels of water stress.

“We can move electricity thousands of miles, but we rarely move water that far, so water is much more of a local issue,” Rhodes said.

Resistance has been fierce. In drought-ridden Utah, for example, thousands of residents pushed back against a proposed 40,000-acre data center project in part over its risks to an already-shrinking lake. Opposition has also swept California, a state that has long been plagued by water challenges, and San Francisco recently approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals.

As scrutiny has intensified, many hyperscalers have rushed to show that they are taking the issue seriously, with an assortment of pledges to reduce water use. But for many companies, there’s a big financial trade-off between using water and using more energy.

“It’s a catch-22 there when it comes to water consumption,” Rhodes said. While there are ways of minimizing water usage in cooling, that generally requires more energy—and firms are financially incentivized to allocate that electricity elsewhere. “The value of the compute is so high, they want to put as much of the electricity into computers and [the] least amount into cooling as they possibly can,” he said.

Land and Pollution

The rapid expansion of data centers has intensified scrutiny over their physical footprint and impacts on nearby communities. More than 40 percent of Americans live within a five-mile radius of at least one existing or planned data center, according to Pew.

All data centers are physically imposing structures, but they vary widely in size. A typical large data center can take up about 250,000 square feet—far eclipsing the size of an American football field.

Some proposed projects, like the aforementioned Utah bid, will now be set on almost 20,000 acres of land—about the size of Manhattan. (In fact, the investor behind the Utah project originally wanted the project to be double that size until fierce backlash forced him to scale back his ambitions.)

While nearly 90 percent of America’s existing data centers were built in urban areas, developers are now looking elsewhere. About two-thirds of planned data centers are in rural areas, while three-quarters of planned construction will be in the South and Midwest, according to Pew, and nearly 40 percent of those will be the first in their respective counties.

As the boom takes off across the country, reports have shed light on the potential fallout for local communities, particularly with regard to pollution. Just last month, one New Jersey data center spilled 5,000 gallons of diesel fuel into a nearby river, raising fears of long-term environmental risks despite cleanup efforts.

There’s also unseen pollution. Residents living near data centers have complained about the incessant noise pollution of the hulking facilities. The data center expansion—and the related natural gas buildout—also threatens harmful pollutants that imperil air quality and pose health risks. Researchers estimate that data centers’ air pollution could cost more than $20 billion in annual public health costs by 2028.

Maxine Davey contributed graphics research.

text:
Agreements with Ameren Illinois, ComEd, and MidAmerican advance the Perry County solar project and the state's energy goals

PERRY COUNTY, Ill. and SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Oct. 13, 2026/PRNewswire/ -- Arevon Energy, Inc., a leading American energy developer, owner, and operator, today announced it has executed three 20-year Indexed Renewable Energy Credit (REC) contracts with Ameren Illinois Company (Ameren Illinois), Commonwealth Edison Company (ComEd), and MidAmerican Energy Company (MidAmerican) for its 200 megawatt (MWac)/275 megawatt (MWdc) Panther Energy Project in Perry County, Illinois.

The Panther Energy Project is anticipated to begin construction in 2027 and reach completion in 2028, creating an estimated 200 construction jobs. The project is expected to contribute an estimated $20 million in property tax payments over its operating life, benefiting area schools, infrastructure, and other public services while driving additional economic activity. Arevon has established a local office in Pinckneyville, providing landowners, residents, and other community members with direct access to the Panther project team during development and upcoming construction. Once operational, the project is expected to generate enough electricity to power more than 37,000 Illinois homes.

The long-term commercial agreements follow Panther Energy's selection in the Illinois Power Agency's (IPA) Summer 2026 Indexed REC procurement, which was approved by the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC). Under the IPA's procurement methodology, Panther Energy was selected to deliver 421,131 RECs in the first year, which will be allocated among Ameren Illinois, ComEd, and MidAmerican through separate long-term contracts with each utility.

The Indexed REC structure provides long-term revenue certainty that supports the development and financing of new renewable energy projects. The RECs acquired by the utilities will help meet their obligations under the Illinois Renewable Portfolio Standard.

The Summer 2026 procurement was conducted pursuant to Illinois's Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA), which became law in 2021 and established the Indexed REC pricing structure for utility-scale renewable energy procurements. In total, the ICC approved contracts for 1.55 gigawatts of new renewable energy capacity, including four utility-scale solar projects totaling 740 MWac, through the Summer 2026 procurement.

"Arevon is proud to work with Ameren Illinois, ComEd, and MidAmerican through the IPA procurement to move Panther Energy closer to construction and contribute to Illinois's energy goals," said Tommy Greer, Chief Commercial Officer at Arevon. "We appreciate the collaboration of Perry County residents, landowners, and local officials throughout the project's development. We look forward to delivering reliable, homegrown energy to the grid while creating jobs, generating long-term economic benefits, and investing in the local community."

Arevon is actively growing its portfolio in the Midwest region of the United States through the operations, construction, and continued development of energy facilities. Recent milestones in the Midwest include the start of operations at its 430 MWdc Kelso Solar Project in Missouri and Ratts 1 and Heirloom Solar Projects in Indiana, which have a cumulative capacity of 264 MWdc. Ratts 1 and Heirloom were awarded the 2025 Proximo North America Solar Deal of the Year. The company has also nearly completed construction on its 124 MWdc Big Muddy Solar Project in Jackson County, Illinois. In addition, Arevon developed and managed construction of the 251 MWdc Gibson Solar Project and the 228 MWdc Posey Solar Project in Indiana on behalf of local utilities.

About Arevon Energy, Inc.

Arevon is a U.S. energy leader committed to powering America with affordable, reliable, and secure homegrown energy. Headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona, and with a regional office in New York City, the company's experienced and dedicated team develops, finances, builds, owns, and operates renewable energy projects nationwide. With a strong track record in utility-scale solar and energy storage, Arevon is a trusted partner to utilities and businesses seeking cost-effective, sustainable energy solutions. By prioritizing American manufacturing and domestic energy production, the company invests in U.S. jobs, strengthens local economies, and advances the country's energy independence.

Arevon owns and operates more than 6.3 gigawatts of solar and energy storage projects across 18 states, is currently constructing 370 megawatts (MW) of new capacity, and maintains a robust development portfolio. The company has also partnered with local utilities to develop and build 480 MW of solar energy, ensuring each project was successfully integrated into their communities. Together, this scale, execution, and ongoing development activity position Arevon at the forefront of American energy innovation. For more information, visit arevonenergy.com.

text:
October 13, 2026 Mactaquac, New Brunswick Natural Resources Canada

The world is changing rapidly. Global trade is upended, wars are ongoing in Europe and the Middle East, artificial intelligence is scaling at speed, and climate change is intensifying. In response, Canada is focused on what we can control: building a prosperous, secure and sustainable Canadian economy. Central to this mission is supplying and controlling our own energy. A reliable, affordable and clean electricity system keeps families’ bills affordable, makes Canadian businesses more competitive and will build a more secure and sustainable Canada for the long term.

That is why, today, the Honourable Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, announced an investment of almost $270 million for clean and reliable energy in New Brunswick. This includes:

A $219-million site development loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) to NB Power for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project to support technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning activities.

Mactaquac Generation Station is New Brunswick’s largest renewable energy asset and NB Power’s largest hydroelectric facility. The 672-megawatt (MW) run-of-river station supplies 30 percent of the province’s renewable energy requirements and 20 percent of its peak electricity demand.

Mactaquac has faced premature concrete deterioration that has affected critical equipment, including turbines and spillway gates. NB Power’s Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a phased rehabilitation program that will enable the generating station to reach its 100-year lifespan.

$50 million from Natural Resources Canada to NB Power for the Static Synchronous Compensator (STATCOM) project at the Salisbury Terminal to strengthen southern New Brunswick’s electricity system.

The Salisbury Terminal is a high-voltage transmission substation that is key to managing the flow of electricity across New Brunswick’s grid. It will improve grid stability and reliability in southern New Brunswick while supporting the integration of additional renewable energy resources as electricity demand continues to grow.

Police removed the protesters, who wore T-shirts bearing the slogan “Make polluters pay.” The protests come as South Africa seeks to expand oil and gas development to attract investment and bolster energy security.

text:
JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Climate activists picketed outside the African Energy Week conference in Cape Town, South Africa, on Tuesday, calling for an end to new oil and gas exploration across the continent and accusing energy companies of prioritizing profits over people and the environment.

Greenpeace Africa and Extinction Rebellion campaigners challenged efforts to position Africa as a new frontier for fossil fuel development, arguing that further investment would worsen climate change and threaten communities already grappling with its effects.

“Oil companies from overseas have made billions in profits this year alone at the expense of people’s lives, at the expense of ecosystems, at the expense of African lives,” Siya Myeza, a climate and energy campaigner with Greenpeace Africa, told The Associated Press.

Myeza branded the gathering “Africa Exploitation Week,” accusing the industry of driving environmental destruction and poverty. Police removed the protesters, who wore T-shirts bearing the slogan “Make polluters pay.”

The protests come as South Africa seeks to expand oil and gas development to attract investment and bolster energy security. The government presents natural gas as a complement to renewable energy, saying gas-fired plants could provide electricity when wind and solar output drops.

Despite legal setbacks, British energy giant Shell plans to drill up to five deepwater wells in the Northern Cape Ultra Deep block off South Africa’s west coast to explore for and assess oil and gas deposits. The project’s environmental approval has drawn appeals.

Protesters say such plans risk prolonging dependence on fossil fuels at a time when countries should be cutting emissions.

Judy Scott-Goldman, a representative of Extinction Rebellion in Cape Town, acknowledged that renewable energy would feature at the conference but said campaigners opposed promoting new oil and gas exploration.

She said expanding fossil fuel use would run counter to commitments under the Paris climate agreement to reduce emissions.

“We’re here to say we don’t want to see any exploration of oil and gas on this continent,” she told the AP.

She pointed to fires, floods and rising food prices as consequences of climate change, warning that its effects could also drive migration and social unrest.

title: Budget 2027: Energy and Infrastructure Expenditure - WILLIAM FRY
description:
The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) has secured €1.28 billion in Budget 2027 to support Ireland’s energy transition, climate action objectives and environmental programmes.
While much attention has focused on affordability measures for households and businesses, Budget 2027 also contains several announcements of particular significance for the energy and infrastructure sector.
While aimed at reducing energy costs and improving energy efficiency, these measures also contribute to the wider decarbonisation of Ireland’s energy system.
Budget 2027 combines continued investment in renewable energy and decarbonisation initiatives with additional resourcing for the regulatory and administrative frameworks that underpin infrastructure development.
For a full briefing of the measures announced across Budget 2027, please see William Fry’s Budget 2027 update here.
text:
The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) has secured €1.28 billion in Budget 2027 to support Ireland’s energy transition, climate action objectives and environmental programmes.

While much attention has focused on affordability measures for households and businesses, Budget 2027 also contains several announcements of particular significance for the energy and infrastructure sector. The Government repeatedly identifies accelerating infrastructure delivery, streamlining regulatory processes and prioritising critical energy infrastructure as key objectives for 2027, indicating that the focus is increasingly shifting from policy formulation to implementation. Additional investment in renewable energy, district heating, biomethane, regulatory capacity and environmental administration indicates a growing recognition that Ireland’s energy transition will depend not only on policy ambition, but on the State’s ability to facilitate infrastructure development and regulatory decision-making at pace.

Energy Transformation Remains the Central Priority

The most significant allocation in Budget 2027 is the provision of more than €950 million to DCEE’s ‘Energy Transformation’ programme, which intends to support the deployment of renewable energy and the delivery of energy efficiency measures across the built environment. This figure includes a record €655 million in capital funding allocated to SEAI home and community energy upgrade schemes, including enhanced supports for solar PV, battery storage, insulation measures and a new boiler scrappage scheme. While aimed at reducing energy costs and improving energy efficiency, these measures also contribute to the wider decarbonisation of Ireland’s energy system. Further, Budget 2027 seeks to encourage greater participation in microgeneration and rooftop solar by increasing the income tax disregard for households exporting electricity to the grid, from €400 to €600.

Biomethane Continues to Gather Momentum

The most notable sector-specific announcement is the confirmation that a €200 million capital grant scheme for biomethane development will open in the coming days. DCEE’s Budget 2027 press release notes that seven anaerobic digestion plants have recently been completed or are under construction, highlighting the growing role of biomethane in Ireland’s long-term energy infrastructure.

Biomethane has increasingly been identified as a key renewable gas solution in Ireland’s decarbonisation strategy, particularly for sectors where full electrification may not be feasible. As discussed in our previous article, Biomethane Production Facilities in Ireland, the development of a large-scale biomethane industry will require not only financial support but also effective planning, environmental and regulatory frameworks capable of facilitating project delivery. The announcement of a dedicated €200 million capital support scheme therefore represents a significant indication of the Government’s commitment to advancing the sector beyond the policy stage and towards project delivery. This investment is also significant in the context of the proposed Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO). Once introduced, the RHO will require suppliers of fossil fuels used for heating to ensure that a proportion of the energy they supply is from a renewable source. The RHO Bill is now at an advanced stage of priority drafting; however, the European Commission has found the Bill’s proposed multiplier for indigenously produced biomethane to be incompatible with EU law. Further detail is set out in our previous article, Ireland’s Renewable Heat Obligation.

Continued Support for District Heating Infrastructure

District heating systems generate heat at a central source and distribute it as hot water through a network of insulated pipes, providing space heating and hot water to homes and businesses. DCEE confirmed that, in addition to the operational district heating network in Tallaght, Dublin, nine projects have received pre-construction funding through the Climate Action Fund. DCEE also announced that €50 to €100 million has been allocated from the Infrastructure Climate and Nature Fund for future district heating projects, with the district heating capital funding scheme expected to open during the first quarter of 2027.

Although the district heating sector is still nascent, it is expected to play an increasingly important role in Ireland’s energy transition with the repeated allocation of public funding demonstrating an ongoing commitment to establishing a pipeline of viable projects. For developers, investors and local authorities, the continued availability of funding is a promising sign that projects will continue to progress from concept stage towards construction and operation.

Increased Resourcing for Maritime and Environmental Regulation

Beyond direct project funding, Budget 2027 also acknowledges the role of regulatory capacity in delivering major infrastructure projects. The allocation of more than €10 million to the Maritime Area Regulatory Authority (MARA) is intended to support the continued development of Ireland’s maritime planning and consenting framework, including administrative reforms aimed at improving the efficiency of decision-making processes. This is particularly significant for the offshore renewable energy sector, where regulatory certainty and timely consenting remain key considerations for developers and investors.

There are set to be further benefits to the offshore renewable energy sector in the form of continued investment in maritime data and mapping infrastructure. The ‘Budget 2027 Expenditure Report’ confirms ongoing support for the INFOMAR marine mapping programme and associated maritime data collection initiatives, which provide important baseline information for offshore development. These investments contribute to the technical and regulatory foundations required to support the delivery of large-scale offshore renewable energy projects.

Additional funding has been allocated to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), with the DCEE highlighting ongoing reforms aimed at improving the efficiency and predictability of licensing processes while maintaining environmental standards. Environmental licences and approvals are often critical path items for project delivery, and greater certainty around regulatory timelines can play an important role in project planning, financing and risk allocation.

A Focus on Delivery

Ireland’s ambitious climate and energy objectives are well publicised. To achieve these aims, the State is focusing its efforts on ensuring that the infrastructure required to meet those objectives can be delivered efficiently and at scale. Budget 2027 combines continued investment in renewable energy and decarbonisation initiatives with additional resourcing for the regulatory and administrative frameworks that underpin infrastructure development.

This funding should not be viewed in isolation and is supported by a pipeline of upcoming new legislation. The Government’s Autumn 2026 Legislation Programme includes several bills that will provide the legal framework for these investments. The Heat (Networks and Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill will establish a regulatory model for district heating, the Offshore Transmission Asset Investment Fund Bill will underpin a €2 billion State equity investment in EirGrid to support offshore grid infrastructure, and the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill has been designated for priority publication (see our recent article, Energy Legislation: What’s Moving This Autumn?). Taken together, these measures demonstrate an increasing focus on implementation and project delivery as the next phase of Ireland’s energy transition.

For a full briefing of the measures announced across Budget 2027, please see William Fry’s Budget 2027 update here.

Contributed by Kate Lyttle

The Climate Action Tracker has just published what it views as two extremely disappointing country analyses: the US ("Critically insufficient"), and Canada ("Highly insufficient"), as both governments roll back climate policies.

The Trump Administration continues its unprecedented rollback of climate mitigation measures (see list below). The CAT still rates the US climate agenda under the Trump Administration as "Critically insufficient".

Prime Minister Mark Carney admits that the country will miss its 2030 and 2035 targets under his plan. Canada continues with a "Highly insufficient" overall rating, but the CAT has downgraded its sub-rating for Canada's Policies & action to "Critically insufficient".

"The Trump Administration continues to escalate the most aggressive, comprehensive, and consequential rollback of climate mitigation targets, policies, and funding that the Climate Action Tracker has ever analysed," said CAT US country lead Finn Hossfeld of CAT partner organisation NewClimate Institute.

In neighbouring Canada, the CAT projected that implemented and planned policies two years ago would cut emissions by 30% below 2005 levels by 2030. With many of those policies now removed or weakened, planned policies are now projected to cut emissions by less than half, to 14%.

"What is shocking to us is the true extent to which Prime Minister Carney has rolled back climate policies, largely in favour of the fossil fuel industry," said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, a CAT partner.

"This Carney climate carnage, while not quite as bad as Trump's, is rapidly heading in the same direction, despite the country being hit by record wildfires and other devastating climate impacts. Based on this assessment, as it presently stands, if the European Union were to import the Canadian policies it would further undermine the EU‘s own climate action," said Hare.
